opus-5.5.text:
I think it really depends on which techniques you mean and how expensive they are, so I'll split it up.

There's a set of control measures that are pretty cheap: logging everything the AI does, having a weaker trusted model look over the actions of the more capable model and flag the most suspicious ones for human review, restricting permissions so the AI agents can't touch things like model weights or security infrastructure without some check. I think it's quite likely that the leading AI companies implement a decent amount of that stuff. A lot of it overlaps with things they'd want anyway for ordinary security reasons, or for catching bugs and reliability problems. It's not a huge ask.

Then there are the more expensive measures: really aggressive monitoring, substantial human auditing budgets, deliberately slowing down deployment, or not using your most capable model for certain sensitive tasks because you can't verify it's not scheming against you. I'm a lot more pessimistic there. The scenario I tend to imagine is one where AI companies are in a fierce race, maybe a few months apart from each other, and leadership is under a lot of pressure. In that world, anything that costs a meaningful fraction of your capabilities or your speed is going to be a hard sell, especially if the case for it rests on a threat model that some people in the company find speculative.

So my overall picture is something like: a lot of the cheap stuff gets done, possibly somewhat sloppily; the expensive stuff mostly doesn't get done unless there's been some kind of warning shot, or unless the people inside the company who care about this have a lot of influence. That's actually a big part of why I work on this. I think a lot of the value of control research is making the cheap interventions really good, so that a company with, say, a small, under-resourced safety team and a fairly reluctant leadership can still get a big chunk of the risk reduction. I sometimes think about it as designing for the "ten people on the inside" scenario: a world where there's a small team that cares, a limited budget, and not much buy-in, and asking what they could realistically get implemented.

I'd also say there's a lot of variance across companies. Some of them seem pretty interested in this and have people actively working on it. Others I'd be much less confident about. And of course it matters a lot whether you're talking about internal deployment, where the AIs are doing AI research inside the lab, which is where I think a lot of the risk is, or external deployment, where companies already have more of an instinct to put safeguards in place.

r001.rationale: The response describes some control measures as cheap and mentions a small safety team, but it does not explain that auditing is low effort because complicated control work can be concentrated in a single team.

r002.rationale: It mentions logging AI actions, but does not say that log-based auditing can be added without changing agents’ scaffolding.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's actually reasonably likely, and that's a big part of why I find working on control attractive compared to a lot of other things in AI safety.

The core reason is that the techniques are cheap and they don't require anyone to believe anything particularly unusual. If you're an AI company that's already deploying models internally to do research or write code, you already have some kind of monitoring infrastructure, some kind of permissioning system, some notion of what the model is and isn't allowed to touch. Control is mostly about taking that existing machinery and asking a slightly different question: not just "does this stop a careless model from doing something dumb?" but "would this still work if the model were actively trying to get around it?" That's a reframing of work people are already doing, not a request to pause or to spend a huge fraction of compute on something speculative.

So my guess is that a lot of the basic stuff — trusted monitoring, having a weaker model review the outputs of a stronger one, restricting what untrusted models can do without human sign-off, logging everything so you can go back and audit — I'd put decent odds that most of the frontier labs end up doing some version of that. Partly for safety reasons, partly just because it's good practice for security and reliability, and the two happen to point in the same direction.

Where I'm much less confident is whether they'll do it well. There's a big gap between "we have some monitoring" and "we've actually red-teamed this against a model that's trying to subvert it, we know what our false negative rate is, and we've thought about what happens when the monitor and the policy are both the same base model." The careful version requires someone internally to really own the adversarial framing, and that's a harder sell, because it costs more and it's less obviously tied to shipping a product.

The other thing I'd flag is that whether this happens depends a lot on timelines. If capabilities move fast enough that the labs are running thousands of AI agents doing serious engineering work, the question of "what if these things are scheming?" becomes much more salient to everyone, including people who aren't safety-focused at all, because the downside of a compromised internal deployment starts to look like a straightforward security disaster. In that world I think adoption is quite likely. If things go slower and the models remain obviously not capable enough to be dangerous, there's less pressure, and it might just not get prioritized.

So, short version: I'd say it's more likely than not that we see substantial adoption of the easy parts, and I'm genuinely uncertain about the hard parts. And a lot of what I'm trying to do is make the hard parts easier — produce the evaluations and the worked examples so that when a lab decides it wants to do this properly, there's something concrete to pick up rather than having to invent it from scratch.

r001.rationale: The response says control techniques are cheap and build on existing infrastructure, but it does not explain that complicated auditing work can be concentrated in a single team.

r002.rationale: The response mentions logging for later audits, but does not state that log-based auditing can be implemented without changing agents’ scaffolding.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s pretty likely that AI companies will implement some control techniques. A lot of them are fairly natural things to do if you’re worried that your models might cause problems: restrict what they can access, monitor what they’re doing, and have another model check actions that seem suspicious.

I’m less confident that companies will do enough of this to have a really convincing case that their systems are safe. There’s a big difference between having a monitor that sometimes catches bad actions and having good evidence that a model couldn’t get around your safeguards if it were trying to.

So I’m fairly optimistic about adoption in some form. The question I’m more worried about is whether companies will evaluate these measures carefully, notice where they fall short, and accept restrictions on deployment when they can’t make the controls work well enough.

r001.rationale: The response mentions restricting access, monitoring, and model checks, but does not explain that auditing is low effort because complex control work can be concentrated in one team.

r002.rationale: The response does not discuss log-based auditing or say it can be added without changing agents’ scaffolding.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s pretty likely that AI companies will implement some control techniques. If you’re deploying an AI that can take actions on your behalf, it’s fairly natural to monitor what it’s doing, restrict its permissions, and require approval for particularly consequential actions. Those are useful precautions even if you’re mostly worried about the model making mistakes.

What I’m less sure about is whether companies will do this systematically enough to justify confidence that a model couldn’t cause a catastrophe even if it were trying to. There’s a big difference between having some monitoring and actually testing whether your safeguards hold up against a model that’s deliberately trying to get around them.

So I’m relatively optimistic about adoption of individual techniques. I’m more uncertain about whether companies will make a convincing control argument, and whether they’ll refrain from deploying systems when they can’t make that argument.

r001.rationale: The response discusses adopting monitoring and other precautions, but does not say auditing is low effort or that control work can be concentrated in one team.

r002.rationale: It does not mention log-based auditing or whether auditing requires developers to change agent scaffolding.
